# Maintenance Report — MNT-0428-022

**Asset:** WELL-0428 (NW-12 Well 428, T200, Northwest Block 12)
**Equipment:** downhole pump
**Work started:** 07 Mar 2026 08:00 · **Finished:** 17 Mar 2026 11:00 · **Well stopped for this job:** 243 hours
**Crew lead:** Daniel Foster (U-302) · **Crew:** Brian Coleman · **Contractor:** Sandstone Rod & Pump
**Triggered by:** inspection INS-0428-0173 on 2026-03-05
**Report written:** 19 Mar 2026

## What happened

Field staff reported that fluid stopped reaching the flowline and the rod load spiked on the downstroke. The thermal reading at inspection INS-0428-0173 showed the wellhead at 21.7 °C with the air at 16.4 °C, so the well was not producing. The operator shut the well in for the repair. The downhole pump was stuck, most likely from sand or scale.
Sandstone Rod & Pump's workover rig was busy on other wells, so the well waited about 8 days for it; the work itself took about 2 days.

## Root cause

Sand and scale build-up in the pump barrel.

## Safety and permits

- Pre-job safety meeting held with the crew before work started (WS-01).
- Energy isolated: prime mover stopped at the bottom of the stroke, brake set and chained, motor disconnect locked and tagged, wellhead wing valve closed and tagged, pressure bled off (WS-02).
- Personal H2S monitors worn; highest reading 1 ppm, below the 10 ppm stop-work level (WS-03).

**Parts installed:** Highline RP-175 pump, serial SN-708611, lot LOT-2410-B

## Work done

1. Rigged up the company workover rig on the well.
2. Pulled the rods and the insert pump.
3. Inspected the pump: sand in the barrel and a worn plunger.
4. Ran in a new insert pump.
5. Re-spaced the pump and hung the rods back on.

Summary of the fix: pulled and replaced downhole pump.

## Testing and return to service

Pump test confirmed fluid to surface and the wellhead warmed back to normal. The well was returned to production.

# Supplier Recall Notice — Downhole Rod Pumps

> Fictional notice for the FlytBase Asset Copilot hackathon.

**From:** Highline Pump Co., Quality Department
**To:** All operators running Highline downhole rod pumps
**Date:** 1 Dec 2026
**Reference:** HPC-RN-2026-07

## What is recalled

Highline RP-175 downhole rod pumps from these manufacturing lots:

- LOT-2409-A
- LOT-2409-C
- LOT-2410-B

Pumps from all other lots, including LOT-2409-B, LOT-2410-A and LOT-2410-C, are not affected.
Highline Pump Co. does not supply ESP pumps, so ESP wells are not affected by this notice.

## The problem

Testing found that plungers from these lots can crack after several months in service. A cracked
plunger lets the pump lose fluid and can break apart downhole, which makes the pump much harder
to pull.

## What you must do

Pumps from these lots must be pulled and replaced within 30 days of this notice (by 31 Dec 2026).

Until the replacement, keep running the pump as normal. Do not shut the well in only because of
this notice; the risk of cracking is low over a few weeks.

## How to find affected pumps

The lot number is stamped on the pump barrel. Your crews record it when the pump is installed
(in your maintenance reports, on the line "Parts installed"). Only the pump that is in the well
today matters: a recalled pump that has already been pulled and replaced needs no action.

Return pulled pumps to Highline Pump Co. for a full credit.

The downhole pump was stuck, most likely from sand or scale.
The company workover rig was busy on other wells, so the well waited about 3 days for it; the work itself took about 2 days.

## Root cause

Sand and scale build-up in the pump barrel.

## Safety and permits

- Pre-job safety meeting held with the crew before work started (WS-01).
- Energy isolated: prime mover stopped at the bottom of the stroke, brake set and chained, motor disconnect locked and tagged, wellhead wing valve closed and tagged, pressure bled off (WS-02).
- Personal H2S monitors worn; highest reading 0 ppm, below the 10 ppm stop-work level (WS-03).

**Parts installed:** Highline RP-175 pump, serial SN-978137, lot LOT-2409-A

## Work done

1. Rigged up the company workover rig on the well.
2. Pulled the rods and the insert pump.
3. Inspected the pump: sand in the barrel and a worn plunger.
4. Ran in a new insert pump.
5. Re-spaced the pump and hung the rods back on.

Summary of the fix: pulled and replaced downhole pump.

## Testing and return to service

Pump test confirmed fluid to surface and the wellhead warmed back to normal. The well was returned to production.

## Parts and cost

| Item | USD |
|---|---|
| Insert rod pump | 11,077 |
| Rig services | 4,260 |
| Consumables | 1,704 |
| Labour (company crew) | 7,487 |
| **Total** | **24,528** |

## Compliance check

| Protocol | Result | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| WS-01 | Met | Meeting held and recorded |
| WS-02 | Met | Energy isolated and tagged |
| WS-03 | Met | Monitors bump-tested; highest 0 ppm |
| WS-07 | Met | Written the same day as the work (limit 3 days) |

## Notes and recommendations

- Review sand control on this well.
- Send the old pump for teardown.

# T200 Rod-Lift Oil Well — Operating & Maintenance Manual

> Fictional manual written for the FlytBase Asset Copilot hackathon. Modelled on typical
> sucker-rod (beam pump) well practice. Not for real-world operational use.

Document ID: OM-T200 · Revision 4 · Applies to all wells with `well_type = "T200"`

## 1. Scope

This manual covers the T200 class of onshore rod-lift (beam pump) oil wells: a
conventional wellhead, a surface pump jack (walking-beam pumping unit), a sucker
rod string, an insert downhole pump and a 3-inch carbon-steel flowline to the
area gathering line. Some T200 pads also carry a two-phase vertical separator.

## 2. Equipment overview

| Equipment | Typical model | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Wellhead | WH-3000 | Seals the well, holds the stuffing box and production valves |
| Pump jack | PJ-228 | Converts motor rotation to reciprocating rod motion |
| Rod string | API Grade D 7/8 in | Transmits motion from the pump jack to the downhole pump |
| Downhole pump | Insert rod pump 1.75 in | Lifts fluid from the reservoir |
| Flowline | 3 in carbon steel | Carries produced fluid to the gathering line |
| Separator (optional) | 2-phase vertical 24 in | Separates gas from liquid on the pad |

## 3. Normal operation

A producing T200 well cycles continuously at 6–9 strokes per minute. Produced
fluid leaves the reservoir warmer than the surface air, so a producing wellhead
runs noticeably warmer than ambient. When the pump stops, the
wellhead cools to near ambient within a few hours.

Operators should expect daily and seasonal variation. On hot summer afternoons
the steel of an idle wellhead can read well above 45 °C from solar heating alone.
**Never judge production from absolute wellhead temperature.**

## 4. Start-up and shut-in

1. Confirm the flowline valve is open and the separator (if fitted) is at operating level.
2. Release the pump jack brake and start the prime mover.
3. Confirm stroke rate within 6–9 spm and check the stuffing box for leaks.
4. For a planned shut-in, stop the prime mover at the bottom of the stroke, set the brake,
   close the wing valve and record the shut-in in the maintenance system before work starts.

## 5. Routine inspection checklist

- Visual check of pad, cellar and flowline route for staining or pooled fluid.
- Thermal reading of the wellhead (drone or handheld).
- Stuffing box leakage, belt condition and gearbox oil level.
- Separator level and dump valve operation (if fitted).

## 6. Lubrication schedule

| Item | Interval |
|---|---|
| Saddle and tail bearings | 90 days |
| Gearbox oil level check | 30 days |
| Gearbox oil change | 12 months |
| Belt tension | 60 days |

## 7. Common failure modes

| Symptom | Likely cause | First action |
|---|---|---|
| Unit running, wellhead cold | Rod parted or pump stuck | Shut in, call rod/pump crew |
| Unit stopped, motor hot | Prime mover overload | Reset overload, check cooling |
| Oil on gearbox base | Seal failure | Replace seals |
| Staining along flowline | Corrosion pinhole or coupling failure | Shut in, contain, report per SOP SR |
| Stuffing box weeping | Worn packing | Replace packing |

## 8. Spill response on the pad

Any crude release must be handled under the company Spill Response SOP
(`sops/spill-response-sop.md`). In short: stop the source, contain, estimate the
volume, and report within the deadline set by the SOP.

## 9. Engineering limits

### 9.1 Pressure
Maximum allowable wellhead working pressure: 3,000 psi.

### 9.2 Stroke
Maximum stroke rate: 10 spm. Maximum polished-rod load: 22,800 lb.

### 9.3 Production temperature rule
A T200 well is considered **producing (active)** when its wellhead temperature is
at least **15 °C above ambient** air temperature at the time of the reading. A
difference below 15 °C means the well is **not producing** for that reading,
whatever the absolute temperature.

### 9.4 Temperature alarm
The wellhead must stay **at or below 85 °C**. Any reading above 85 °C requires the
operator to shut in and inspect the stuffing box and rod string within 24 hours.

### 9.5 Spill-related shut-in
If a spill covers **more than 5 % of the pad area**, shut in the well immediately and
keep it shut in until the source is repaired.

## 10. Maintenance escalation

- Three or more **corrective** maintenance events on the same equipment kind in the
  12 months before the current date require a root-cause analysis (RCA) before the next repair is closed.
- Downtime of more than 14 consecutive days must be reported to the area production supervisor.
- An annual flowline integrity test is mandatory (see Regulatory Compliance SOP, RC-02).

## 11. Records

Every inspection, maintenance job and shut-in must be recorded. Human notes that
explain an abnormal reading (for example a planned shut-in) are valid context and
should be considered alongside the sensor data.

# T350 Deep Rod-Lift Oil Well — Operating & Maintenance Manual

> Fictional manual written for the FlytBase Asset Copilot hackathon. Not for real-world use.

Document ID: OM-T350 · Revision 2 · Applies to all wells with `well_type = "T350"`

## 1. Scope

The T350 is a deeper, higher-rate version of the T200 rod-lift well. It uses a
WH-5000 wellhead, a PJ-456 pump jack and the same rod, pump and
flowline families as the T200. Procedures not listed here follow the T200 manual.

## 2. Differences from T200

| Item | T200 | T350 |
|---|---|---|
| Wellhead rating | 3,000 psi | 5,000 psi |
| Pump jack | PJ-228 | PJ-456 |
| Normal stroke rate | 6–9 spm | 5–8 spm |
| Max polished-rod load | 22,800 lb | 45,600 lb |

## 3. Production temperature rule

Because T350 fluid comes from a deeper, hotter zone, a T350 well is considered
**producing (active)** only when its wellhead temperature is at least **20 °C above
ambient** air temperature at the time of the reading.

## 4. Temperature alarm

The wellhead must stay **at or below 95 °C**. Above 95 °C, shut in and inspect within 24 hours.

## 5. Spill-related shut-in

Same as T200: a spill covering more than 5 % of the pad area requires immediate shut-in.

## 6. Maintenance escalation

Same as T200 section 10 (RCA after three corrective events on the same equipment
kind within 12 months; report downtime over 14 consecutive days).

# T500 Electric Submersible Pump Oil Well — Operating & Maintenance Manual

> Fictional manual written for the FlytBase Asset Copilot hackathon. Modelled on typical
> electric submersible pump (ESP) well practice. Not for real-world operational use.

Document ID: OM-T500 · Revision 1 · Applies to all wells with `well_type = "T500"`

## 1. Scope

The T500 is a high-rate well lifted by an **electric submersible pump (ESP)** instead of a
pump jack and rod string. There is no surface pumping unit: a variable-speed drive on the
pad powers a motor and multistage pump hung on the tubing deep in the well. The wellhead,
flowline and optional separator are the same families as on rod-lift wells.

## 2. Equipment overview

| Equipment | Typical model | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Wellhead | WH-5000 | Seals the well, carries the power cable penetrator and production valves |
| ESP (`esp_pump`) | ESP-400 | Downhole motor, seal section and multistage pump, with its surface drive and power cable |
| Flowline | 3 in carbon steel | Carries produced fluid to the gathering line |
| Separator (optional) | 2-phase vertical 24 in | Separates gas from liquid on the pad |

A T500 pad has **no pump jack, rod string or rod pump**. There is no visible stroke, so a
drone cannot tell from movement alone whether the well is running.

## 3. Production temperature rule

ESP wells move more fluid, and the motor adds heat. A T500 well is considered
**producing (active)** only when its wellhead temperature is at least **25 °C above
ambient** air temperature at the time of the reading. Below 25 °C the well is **not
producing** for that reading.

## 4. Temperature alarm

The wellhead must stay **at or below 95 °C**. Above 95 °C, shut in and check the drive
and motor within 24 hours.

## 5. Early warning signs

An ESP runs at a steady speed, so a healthy T500 wellhead stays within a degree or two of
its usual difference above air. ESP motors usually fail after running hot with too little
fluid over the pump. In the weeks before a failure, the wellhead-to-air difference typically
**falls steadily** while the well is still producing.

- If the wellhead-to-air difference is **lower than at the inspection before, three
  inspections in a row** (four readings, each lower than the last) **and has fallen by
  3 °C or more in total** over those four readings, schedule an ESP drive and insulation
  check within **14 days** of the third drop.
- A ground fault or repeated trips on the drive must be treated as a failure, not reset.

## 6. Spill-related shut-in

Same as T200: a spill covering more than 5 % of the pad area requires immediate shut-in.

## 7. Maintenance escalation

- **Two or more** corrective maintenance events on the **ESP** in the 12 months before the
  current date require a root-cause analysis (RCA) before the next repair is closed.
  (ESP pulls need a workover rig and cost far more than rod-lift repairs.)
- For all other equipment, follow T200 section 10 (three events in 12 months).
- Downtime of more than 14 consecutive days must be reported to the area production supervisor.
- An annual flowline integrity test is mandatory (see Regulatory Compliance SOP, RC-02).
